newsitem.title: USA: Mountain states, South lead among entrepreneurs.
newsitem.headline: Mountain states, South lead among entrepreneurs.

text.p: Despite the mythic proportions of Silicon Valley as the start-up centre of the United States, a new report says the hottest spots for budding entrepreneurs are in the Mountain states and the South.

Indeed, California ranked 18th among states, according to the study from Cognetics, a Cambridge, Mass.-based research firm, and the Silicon Valley/San Francisco Bay Area region ranked 31st among metropolitan areas for nurturing start-ups.
Utah was at the top of the list among states, with Salt Lake City-Provo the No. 1 metropolitan area.
The study's main aim was to compare places in terms of how successful they were in fostering start-ups, rather than the aggregrate growth rates of the area's economy.
So the group measured the number of firms started in the last 10 years that employ at least five people currently.
It also looked at firms that grew significantly over the past four years that were relatively young -- less than 10 years old -- at the beginning of the period.
What it found was that "both the Mountain and South Atlantic regions continued to hold on to their No. 1 and No. 2 spots, respectively."
Among states, Arizona came after Utah, followed by Nevada, Alabama, and Virginia.
Following Salt Lake City-Provo among cities was Atlanta, Birmingham-Tuscaloosa, Ala., Phoenix, and the Washington, DC, region.
Looking at smaller metropolitan areas, the top five were Las Vegas; Huntville, Ala.; Austin, Texas; Boise, Idaho; and Albuquerque, N.M.
It also found significant growth of young companies in rural areas, such as southern Alabama, the Puget Sound region of Washington, and Maine.

"The idyllic notion in many American heads is to bail out of the big-city rat race, and use modern technology (fax, computers, modem, electronic mail, telephone switching, online services, the Internet) to set up shop in 'the country.'
In these rural areas, the Western and Southern states dominated.
The reason starts-up congregate in certain places has little to do with cost, the report said. "In fact, if there is any pattern, it is a shift to higher, rather than lower, cost areas," it said.
The companies locate where they do because they are searching for high quality, with the biggest factors being universities, a skilled labour pool, airports and a nice place to live.
Part of this reflects the fact that many of these start ups are in the knowledge or service industries that can virtually locate anywhere -- but which need to travel easily to visit clients.
"It is not an accident that nine of the top 10 most entrepreneurial, larger metro areas are hub airports," the report said.
